newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada financial markets end stronger after Martin.
newsitem.headline: Canada financial markets end stronger after Martin.

text.p: Canadian financial markets ended mostly stronger on Wednesday, reacting positively to Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin's annual update on the country's economic and financial situation.
Canadian bonds, T-bills, equities and the currency strengthened after the update, with bonds and T-bills ending the day stronger.
Martin appeared before the House of Commons finance committee today at 1530 EDT/1930 GMT to update the country's economic and fiscal situation for fiscal 1995-96 ended March 31.
In the update, Martin confirmed expectations he surpassed his 1995/96 budget deficit target of C$32.7 billion. Martin said the deficit came in at C$28.6 billion, or C$4.1 billion below expectations.

"What it drove home is how much better this year's number and next year's number are going to be because of lower interest rates. In fact, he may be a year ahead of his programs," said Michael Manford, chief economist with Scotia Capital Markets.
Martin also forecast a 1998/99 deficit of C$9.0 billion or about 1.0 percent of gross domestic product, and said a broad-based tax cut now would be wrong.
"I think his insistence that he won't cut taxes strengthens the market's view of the government's resolve to stay the course," said Manford. "It's also very bullish for the Canadian dollar."
The Canadian dollar ended firmer at C$1.3624 (US$0.7395) from Tuesday's close of C$1.3536 (US$0.7388). The currency had been trading at about C$1.3533 (US$0.7389) before Martin began speaking.
Dealers said earlier weakness was erased by Martin's speech and the broad optimism about Canada's economy is expected to continue overnight with buying from Asia and Europe.
Canadian bonds and T-bills rallied following Martin's speech, outperforming their U.S. counterparts.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.10 to C$106.30 to yield 7.451 percent, compared to the U.S. 30-year benchmark which fell 11/32 to yield 6.83 percent.
The spread between the two bonds fell to its lowest level in 11 years, narrowing to 62 basis points from 66 at Tuesday's close.
The yield on the three-month, when-issued T-bill fell to 3.40 percent from 3.41 percent at Tuesday's close, further pricing in a interest rate cut by the Bank of Canada.
Canadian equities, which were weaker ahead of Martin's address, pared losses to end the day flat. Analysts said they expect equities to get a boost from the country's improving finances.

The benchmark Toronto Stock Exchange 300 Index slipped 0.41 point to close at 5436.13 in heavy turnover of 100.3 million shares valued at C$1.6 billion. The TSE 300 had been down 5.74 basis points at 5,430.80 before Martin's speech.
